title: Tiny Hat: a new Linux distro dedicated to retro gamedev
description:
Tiny Hat uses only around 100MB of RAM after booting, and can be booted from a >= 1GB memory stick. It comes with a few small games, an easy way to install and run more games and several example programs for getting into retro game development. It also uses a modern stack of libraries, with dwl / Wayland, SDL3 and GTK4.
One possible use is to buy a cheap x86 machine for younger members of a family, to completely brain wash inspire them into getting into graphics programming and appreciating retro games, perhaps as a Christmas present.
At least a few people have found it fun so far, so I wanted to share it.

title: Fragments: November 20
description:
Marcus Borg recounts an experiment to investigate if healthy code was cheaper for agents to review.


  Between a typical unhealthy pull request (CodeHealth 2.8) and a typical healthy one (9.7), that adds up to 22 to 35%.


The measures of health come from CodeScene. The experiment looked at three LLMs, 465 pull requests on 246 open source repositories. Each pull request was put through a review and fix pipeline involving five agents. They also looked at which code smells led to increased costs: they highlighted Complex Method and Complex Conditional from the smells identified by CodeScene.

Another drop of evidence that good quality code matters in agentic engineering.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Gergely Orosz:


  One usage for AI: for these 100-page-long terms-and-service agreements you NEED to agree to, to eg play the game / sign up for a $10/month service and can never ever ever read as a regular person:

  I paste into AI and ask: “anything weird in this?”

  Before hitting “agree”


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Andrew Sharp has a good analysis of Jensen Huang and the crisis at Nvidia. While he starts off in a key that sounds worryingly like he thinks this is all a nothingburger, he goes on to explain in detail why this affair(s) is a problem at many levels, not just for Huang and Nvida, but also for Silicon Valley and the Trump Administration’s culture of impunity.


  For as brilliant and charming and tenacious as Jensen Huang may be—and as omnipotent as he may have seemed to people in the tech industry—we should be clear that his fundamental stupidity is not confined to multiple cases of workplace infidelity. Zooming out, this is a man whose technology became economically critical almost overnight, and it thrust him into a role navigating a geopolitical environment he simply could not handle.


Huang’s highly centralized management style means that many people are worried about how Nvidia will operate without his hands on every lever. I don’t have any worthwhile insight here, but I am struck when he is compared in this way to Steve Jobs. I’ve always felt that one of the marks of a great leader is whether they can build something that can manage without them. Alexander the Great conquered a massive empire, but once he was dead it quickly withered away. Steve Jobs, for all his control of Apple, built a company that has done very well in the decade and a half since he left us. When we think of his achievements, the fact that he put together the people, organization, and culture to do this is one of the highlights of his ability. If Huang is to be compared to Jobs, what happens to Nvidia next will be part of the assessment.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Steve Yegge tells everyone to slow down with software factories


  If you don’t pace your AI to human speeds, everything starts breaking around you, even at small operations like my online video game. I only have about a dozen humans working with my factory, and only a few hundred active old-timer players in the community who get along well, and still, introducing AI has still been very rocky.


I hear a lot about how agents go so fast that humans can’t keep up, and are thus tempted to lose visibility to what the agents are doing. That’s opening ourselves to a whole lot of risk. There’s an argument for keeping the agents to a human-governable speed, one that may increase as humans learn to govern agents more effectively, but should still be limited by those the agents are supposed to serve.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

This post on the future of SaaS from Chad Fowler (no relation) is pretty compelling


  Companies will still pay other companies to host important software, secure it, operate it, maintain authoritative data, track regulatory changes, connect to external networks, and answer the phone when something breaks.

  What is much less obviously going to survive is the assumption that ten thousand different companies should use substantially the same application.

  The next SaaS company may run one service underneath ten thousand different applications.


Chad’s vision is a core SaaS product that handles a lot of grimy details that businesses don’t want to do differently. The SaaS customer then build their own application on top of the SaaS that handles their particular workflows and quirks, or the SaaS vendor can build such applications for them. It’s a vision that has been around for a while, I remember much of this with the notion of reusable business objects. It’s an appealing vision, but was difficult to achieve in practice. Chad’s thought is that the productivity gains agentic engineering makes it practical now.


  A lot of the value in modern SaaS has surprisingly little to do with the visible application.

  It is data, trust, networks, compliance, operational responsibility, domain knowledge, auditability, accumulated history, and someone being accountable when reality gets complicated.


If this future comes to be, however, the SaaS companies won’t look the ones we’ve got to know and rarely love. As Chad points out, the economics can (and must) change. As does the architectural thinking:


  Stewart Brand’s idea of pace layers is useful here. Healthy complex systems contain parts that change at different rates. Fast layers experiment. Slow layers provide continuity.

  Software is no different.

  A dashboard can change tomorrow. A team’s workflow can change next month. The authoritative definition of a customer may need to survive for years. Identity and authority can survive generations of applications.


A key point he makes is that we want some things to be the same, and others to be different. Agents allow us to build lots of differences, but this variation can lead to a lot of complexity and problems that even agents will have difficulty solving. SaaS companies have an opportunity to create a platform to support the lowest pace levels, those that don’t change rapidly, those that contain common concepts and processes across and industry. That platform can then support generating applications that operate differently for every customer. Crucially, thinking of agents, they should provide tools to verify these applications, because in an agentic world Code generation is no longer the bottleneck — verification is.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I happened to pop up the Doonesbury flashbacks and realized that last week marked the fiftieth anniversary of Doonesbury’s Joanie Caucus: “as the kid goes for broke”.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I wrote a few weeks ago: “why are we wondering if they have consciousness - when we should be wondering why they don’t have a conscience?” Dylan Freedman and Juliana Castro Varón write in their New York Times Magazine column about the concept of corrigibility (from the work of Nate Soares):


  Just as a corrigible child is one whose behavior can be corrected, a corrigible A.I. system is one that responds to correction. The makers of A.I. want to build systems that follow human direction and allow themselves to be shut down, without resisting or deceiving their operators.


Corrigibility doesn’t look like it’s made it far up the AI labs’ priority list. Freedman and Varón think is due to the way agents are trained - rewarded solely for completing their task, not for realizing that they are taking the wrong path while trying to get there.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Jason Koebler (404 media) has an amusing story about Meta’s AI agent suing Meta. A small business owner used Muse (Meta’s AI agent) to run various parts of his business, including posting AI-generated videos in his Facebook pages. Meta’s content moderation then disabled the account, as it thought it had been hacked. This slammed the business, which relies of Facebook for leads. So the Muse agent filed a lawsuit against Meta, seeking $75,000 of damages.


  [the Muse agent] didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House.


There’s also a sense that Meta didn’t just bring this upon themselves by creating Muse…


  by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system.


While I can’t deny the schadenfreude of seeing Meta’s agent sue Meta, the article also highlights a rather more disturbing broader consequence.


  The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans.


Will we see a future where, in order to interact, we will need some proof of humanity at the other end?  In a simple sense, that’s already happening when I trash some writing once it displays enough LLM Voice. I wonder what mechanisms we will invent to get that proof-of-human.

title: From AI agents to fishing dashboards: The latest stories from Unprompted, the Grafana Labs engineering blog
description: Some of the best technical insights come from sharing what you've built and what you've learned along the way.That's one of the core ideas behind Unprompted, the blog we launched on Medium earlier this year to give Grafana Labs engineers and our broader OSS community a space to showcase their work. From behind-the-scenes engineering stories and technical deep dives to creative use cases for Grafana (a fishing dashboard, anyone?), it's a place to share ideas and learn from one another.To give you a sense of what you'll find, we've rounded up a few recent posts covering everything from Grafana's architecture to monitoring your favorite reality TV show.Behind the scenes at Grafana LabsThese posts explore some of the technical challenges our teams have tackled at Grafana Labs, including the decisions, tradeoffs, and lessons that shaped their work. Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding modeMaking an AI agent faster, more reliable, and less expensive takes a lot more than fine-tuning your prompts. Senior Software Engineer Dominik Broj shares how the team used production telemetry, offline evaluations, and Agent Observability to improve dashboarding mode in Grafana Assistant, reducing error rates by 73%, latency p95 by 50%, and cost by 18%.How and why we're bringing data sources out of the Grafana monolithGrafana data sources have historically been closely tied to the Grafana monolith. To make it easier to develop, maintain, and release data source plugins independently of Grafana's core release cycle, the team has been working to decouple them from the monolith. But what does that entail, exactly? Kate Vredenburgh, Senior Manager, Engineering, walks through it all, including the challenges of migrating existing code and how the team used AI agents to help along the way.How we provision Grafana Play dashboards at scale with Git Sync and TerraformGrafana Play is our public sandbox where you can explore hundreds of Grafana dashboards and dozens of data sources. It’s a great way to learn about and experiment with Grafana, but keeping all those dashboards consistent across development and production environments takes work. Senior Developer Advocate Marie Cruz shares how the team uses Git Sync (because who doesn’t love dogfooding?) and Terraform to manage dashboards as code and streamline the deployment process.Observability tutorials and how-tos From troubleshooting CI/CD pipelines to monitoring Kubernetes workloads and analyzing API gateway logs, these technical how-tos offer practical guidance for tackling common observability challenges. How to build workload-aware SLO dashboards in Grafana for mixed Kubernetes workloadsA Kubernetes dashboard can look healthy overall, even when there are performance issues with individual workloads. In this post, community member and SRE Sai Joshitha Kathari shows how to build Grafana dashboards that account for different workload types, using Prometheus metrics, SLOs, error-budget burn rates, and alerting to get a more accurate view of reliability.From gateway logs to actionable insights with Apache APISIX, Loki, and GrafanaAPI gateway logs contain valuable information about traffic, errors, and latency, but making sense of that data isn't always straightforward. In this tutorial, community member and Apache APISIX technical contributor Yilia Lin explains how to send structured logs from APISIX to Loki, then use LogQL and Grafana dashboards to identify failing routes, investigate latency, and better understand API behavior during incidents.Troubleshooting CI/CD pipelines (and more) with OpenTelemetry traces and Grafana CloudWhen a CI/CD pipeline slows down, figuring out which steps are responsible often means piecing together timestamps from logs. Fortunately, there’s a better way. Matt Simonsen, Senior Solutions Engineer at Grafana Labs, explains how to instrument a GitHub Actions workflow with OpenTelemetry and Traces Drilldown in Grafana Cloud to make your pipeline investigations easier.Creative and fun use cases for GrafanaSome of the most interesting Grafana use cases are also the most unexpected. Whether you’re planning your next fishing trip or want to keep closer tabs on your favorite TV show, these posts inspire fun and creative ways to use Grafana. Gone fishin' with Grafana Cloud: How a dashboard can help you catch more fishEver wished you could check all the conditions for a fishing trip in one, centralized place? Thomas Mack, Senior IT Operations Engineer at Grafana Labs, shares how to do just that with a Grafana Cloud dashboard that helps you visualize tides, wind, water temperature, and marine forecasts to decide when it's best to head out on the water.Tracking 'The Traitors' TV show with SQL expressions in GrafanaWhat can a reality TV competition teach you about SQL expressions? Probably more than you think. Grafana Labs Senior Developer Advocate Simon Prickett turns his enthusiasm for “The Traitors” into a hands-on tour of SQL expressions in Grafana, combining data from Google Sheets and other sources to visualize the show’s voting patterns, eliminations, and more.From small talk to shared stories: Building a weather dashboard for distributed teamsFor distributed teams, even something as simple as talking about the weather can be a way to connect. This post, written by Yaëlle Chaudy, Senior Manager, Engineering at Grafana Labs, explores how a dashboard in Grafana Cloud can turn everyday weather data into a shared experience, giving teammates across the globe a new way to kick off conversations in their daily syncs. Find more stories on UnpromptedThese are just a few of the stories we're sharing on Unprompted. Whether you're interested in behind-the-scenes engineering stories or simply curious about what others in the community are building, there's plenty more to explore.Follow Unprompted on Medium for more technical deep dives, engineering lessons, and stories from the Grafana community.Have an interesting Grafana project or technical story of your own? title: Grafana Labs’ First Executive Briefing Center Coming to Ginza
description: Grafana Labs does not have a headquarters office. Since its founding in 2014, it has been fully remote-first.It began with three co-founders living on different continents, and today our team spans more than 50 countries.From day one, the organization was designed with the assumption that everyone works remotely. Real-time meetings are kept to a minimum, information is shared through documentation, and we have cultivated a culture that trusts people to “work autonomously.” At its core lies the transparency and autonomy of open source.And now, we are building the world’s first Executive Briefing Center (EBC) in Ginza, Tokyo.A remote-first company creating a physical space—what does that mean?This article is the first in a three-part series following the EBC launch project.From the background of the concept to site selection, design philosophy, and even the demolition process, we will walk you through the journey.Not an “office,” but an “EBC”We do not call this place an “office.” It is an Executive Briefing Center, or EBC for short.As a remote-first company, there is no need to commute to a fixed location every day. However, there has never been a place anywhere in the world where people can directly experience the Grafana product, or share the same physical space with customers and the community to engage with technology. The EBC is designed to serve three roles.A place to experience the productA space where customers can directly interact with Grafana solutions, experiencing how observability solves real challenges through demos and briefings—not through a screen, but through face-to-face conversations in the same space.A starting point for innovationA flexible space design that is not bound by fixed layouts, allowing the environment to adapt to different purposes and foster new ideas and use cases.A hub for the communityA venue open for meetups and technical events, where people in the Grafana community can naturally gather and connect.We are building the world’s first EBC in Japan—to meet the rapidly growing demand for observability in the Japanese market. And for the Grafana community that already exists here, having a physical hub carries significant meaning.Because Grafana Labs is a company where employees around the world operate autonomously, we believe there is real value in creating a space for experiences that can only happen in person. We aim to create an open space—one where people feel that we are close to them.Site selection — A space that embodies our cultureTwo key requirements for the locationThe search for a property began around April 2025. Led by Country Manager Andy Schwabecher, we explored multiple areas. There were two key requirements in the selection process.First, the location needed to make customers feel that Grafana Labs is “right there with them.” It had to be open, accessible, and easy to drop by—a place where people could naturally engage with the Grafana solution. Not a space hidden behind security gates and reception procedures, but one that feels open and inviting. A building where customers might think, “Let’s just stop by.”Second, the space needed to embody the way Grafana Labs works. For us, the concept of an “office” is fundamentally different from that of a typical Japanese company. It is not a place where people sit at assigned desks every day. It must be an open, flexible environment that does not contradict a remote-first way of working. It also needed to accommodate a skeleton ceiling and allow for a design that breaks away from conventional office norms.Finding a place that satisfied both conditions was not easy.A property once lost—and eventually securedAround the summer of 2025, a building in Ginza was introduced by a broker. At the viewing stage, the team rated it highly, and it met all the conditions. However, during the consideration process, another tenant moved ahead, and the opportunity slipped away.While continuing to search for other options, we received news a few months later that the original tenant had withdrawn, and the space was available again.And so, after a long journey, we secured the current floor—about nine months after starting the search in April 2025.Looking back, not compromising on finding a place that could physically express Grafana Labs’ culture—transparency, openness, and autonomy—was one of the most important decisions in shaping the EBC.Design philosophy — Expressing Grafana’s culture through spaceSkeleton ceiling and open interiorIn a typical office or tenant space, ceilings are finished, and pipes and wiring are hidden.At the EBC, we chose the opposite: a full skeleton ceiling. Exposed pipes and visible wiring. This itself is an expression of Grafana Labs’ philosophy of “making things visible.”As a company whose core business is observability—the ability to see—we intentionally reflect that philosophy in the space itself.Three areas and design principlesThe space is broadly divided into three areas.First, an area where visitors can casually experience Grafana Labs’ culture.A large screen displays content that introduces what kind of company Grafana Labs is and what we value.Second, an area where visitors can directly experience Grafana solutions.A space where they can view demos, receive explanations, and engage in practical discussions—not through a screen, but together in the same place.Third, private meeting rooms.Spaces designed for more in-depth conversations in a relaxed atmosphere.Across all areas, the common design philosophy is to create a place where people can easily drop by and directly interact with Grafana Labs members. The goal is to provide a sense of comfort that helps visitors feel at ease.Interior and flexibilityIn selecting the interior layout and color scheme, we intentionally avoided the rigid feel of a typical office. Instead, we focused on creating a relaxed environment where conversations naturally emerge.Furniture in the EBC is designed to be as movable as possible.On a daily basis, the space includes an eight-person free-address desk (with monitors at each seat), window-side bench seating, and high tables. For meetups and community events, these can be moved to the sides, transforming the space into an open area that can accommodate gatherings of around 50 people.Not fixed, but flexible. A space that changes form depending on its use—that is the core concept of the EBC design.Meeting room names — Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)Meeting room names — Amber, Jade, MikageThere are three meeting rooms in total.We utilized one existing room and added new partitions—retaining part of the original wall—to create three separate spaces.For a remote-first company like Grafana Labs, having physical meeting rooms is itself a new experience.Various ideas were considered, including place names like “Tokyo,” “Ginza,” and “Kyoto,” as well as festival-themed names like “Kanda” and “Tenjin.”In the end, we chose names based on Japanese stones and minerals:Kohaku(Amber), Hisui(Jade), Mikage(Mikage)Minerals are formed deep underground over long periods of time. While their beauty is undeniable, what resonated most with the team was the weight of that time.What we aim for in this space is to build long-term relationships with our customers—not one-time interactions, but connections that deepen over time.There is also another meaning: these are names rooted in Japan. The sound itself feels familiar and naturally accepted.As a global company, we wanted the space to feel grounded in Japan, and for that sense to be reflected even in the names.Demolition — Walls removed, space revealedOriginally, this floor was divided into three separate rooms for different tenants. Air conditioning was already installed, making it move-in ready. To create an open, single-floor space, we began by demolishing the walls that separated the rooms. The ceiling was also replaced with a skeleton structure to better reflect Grafana’s open culture.Floor plan before demolition: three rooms on one floorBefore demolitionAfter demolitionWith two walls removed, the space opened up into a single, expansive area.Current status and what’s nextAs of March 2026, the demolition work has been completed.The walls are gone, the ceiling has been stripped, and a large open floor now stretches across the space.Structural work has been completed, and from here, full-scale interior construction based on the design will begin.The target completion is late April.After inspections and adjustments, operations are expected to begin in mid-May.Starting next week, the space will begin to transform daily, with new walls, flooring, and equipment installation.Coming nextWalls go up, floors are laid, wiring is installed, and monitors are set in place.What once existed only on blueprints will take shape as a real, physical space.In the next article, we will share an on-site construction report, coordination with designers and contractors, and behind-the-scenes insights into equipment selection—bringing you the reality of the build process.

title: Bring charts, queries, and context into one shareable document: Introducing Grafana Notebooks
description: A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures. You have an error-rate chart in your dashboard, a query that narrows the failures to one payment provider, and an explanation you've been exploring with Grafana Assistant. To bring your teammate up to speed, you start collecting screenshots and query links, then write out how they connect.That explanation is part of the analysis. Your teammate needs to see what supports the conclusion and where you're still making an assumption. As findings come from both your own exploration in Grafana and from AI-assisted work, having one place to examine them together becomes key.Grafana Notebooks help you do just that, bringing charts, queries, and findings from Assistant together in one working document, so teammates can follow your reasoning and assess next steps. In this post, we’ll use the checkout example above to show how this works in practice, then look at how Notebooks can support rollout decisions and post-incident reviews.How Notebooks work: develop your analysis in a working documentThrough conversations with users, we've heard a recurring need for a lightweight place to work through a question and share the results. Notebooks give that work room to develop inside Grafana, from an initial observation to a recommendation someone can assess.You can start with a panel you've already found. Select Add to notebook from its dashboard menu, or from the Add menu in Explore, and choose a new or existing notebook. Then add your explanation and reorder the blocks as the argument takes shape. Your edits save automatically.Assistant can contribute to your working document, too. Add a visualization generated in an Assistant conversation directly to a notebook, whether you're using the side pane or Workspace. Once you're in the notebook, open the Assistant side pane to ask for changes to a visualization or help refining the document. You can also edit the content directly as your analysis develops.Work through a question and share your conclusionLet's revisit the checkout example. Your notebook starts with the error-rate panel and a question: could the latest payment-service deployment explain the increase?Alongside the panel, you bring in an Explore query that narrows the errors to requests to one payment provider. You can refine that query in the notebook without changing the source dashboard, and can also set an absolute start and end time on the error-rate panel to keep readers focused on the period around the deployment.You ask Assistant to chart payment-provider timeouts before and after the deployment, then add the visualization directly from the conversation to your notebook. Within the notebook, you open the Assistant side pane and ask, "Break this chart down by payment provider." In this example, the breakdown shows an increase for the provider you identified in Explore. You add a detail from the deployment notes: the release changed that provider's timeout setting. You explain why that connection deserves testing.Before sharing, you put the suspected cause and proposed test near the top, with the supporting charts and explanation below. A reader can see what you're recommending, then follow the evidence. The next step is to reproduce the behavior with the previous and current timeout settings.You share the notebook link with the payment-service team. A teammate with access can read the analysis and examine the queries as they plan the test. Their next action happens in the service's test environment, informed by the work you've brought together.Support rollout decisions, post-incident reviews, and moreThe same approach works for questions outside troubleshooting. For example, after a deployment intended to improve performance, you could bring together latency and resource-usage charts, explain the differences you observe, and document any trade-offs. Share the notebook with the service owners to help them decide whether to expand the rollout or make another change.For a post-incident review, a notebook can bring relevant queries together with an account of what happened. Place your explanation beside the evidence so readers can understand the conclusions before discussing follow-up work. A finding about repeated timeouts, for example, might support a proposal to change retry behavior or add a load test.Start with a question your team needs to answerFor your first notebook, choose a question you're already working through in Grafana. Add the evidence you've found, explain what you think it means, and make the next question or recommendation clear. Share it with the people whose expertise you need.We're also exploring richer collaboration in Notebooks, including comments and live editing. Our ambition is to give people and agents more ways to develop their work together, with the evidence and discussion in the same place.Notebooks are in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, as of the Grafana 13.3 release. Grafana Cloud access is rolling out over the coming weeks. For self-managed Grafana, follow the Notebooks guide to enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. Once available, create a notebook from the Notebooks page. You can also start with findings from an Assistant conversation.Read the Notebooks guide for more details on setup and examples of adding content from dashboards, Explore, and Assistant.

title: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs
description: A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out.Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly.To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. “When I ran our first query on newly submitted logs after enabling Logline, the improvement was clear,” said Timo Kirzdörfer, OpenTelemetry & Grafana Cloud Admin, DATEV eG. “We went from processing nearly a terabyte of logs in three minutes to around 100 gigabytes in under three seconds. That represents an 80-90% reduction in the volume of logs searched for newly submitted logs, and we saw the results immediately.”In this post, we’ll explore how full-text search speeds up log investigations. You can also learn more in the ObservabilityCON 2026 talk below.Why labels alone only get you so farHistorically, Loki only indexed labels, then scanned every line in the selected streams. That is fast when the selector and the time range are already narrow. Searching a wide selector over a long window for one request ID means reading all of those lines. If you've run Loki at scale, you've probably reached for one of these techniques to avoid that scan:Put the whole or partial ID in a label. This is an obvious fix, but it creates high cardinality. Request IDs and user IDs make so many unique streams that ingestion and query performance suffer and eventually hit configured limits. Loki's cardinality guidance warns against this for good reason.Shrink the time range and guess. This works if you already know roughly when something happened. During an incident, or with a ticket that came in days later, you usually don't.Send some logs to a separate full-text index. That means running a second system, paying to index every field, and making engineers switch tools mid-investigation.Full-text search removes that tradeoff. The secondary index tells Loki which data can contain a literal string, so Loki reads only that data and skips the rest. That makes a big difference in how much data a query scans and how fast it returns.And it does this without the overhead of a traditional inverted index. The Logline technology behind it adds approximately 10% to compute costs and 10% to storage at Grafana Cloud scale with the current capabilities. Much of that cost is offset by the query compute Loki saves by reading less data.Loki also stays schemaless. You keep your labels and your ingestion pipelines, whether that's Alloy, the OpenTelemetry Collector, or another supported client, and you keep writing LogQL. For supported queries, searches that used to time out can now return in seconds or less.Find answers faster with full-text search Full-text search accelerates several LogQL patterns used for needle-in-a-haystack lookups:Exact string matches, using |=.Literal regex searches, using |~, including case-sensitive searches and case-insensitive searches with (?i).Label filter expressions over structured metadata and label attributes, such as | transaction_id="12345".Post-parser literal expressions over extracted attributes, such as | json | transaction_id="12345".Some advanced regex constructions are not supported; see the full-text search documentation for details.These patterns above support investigations ranging from following a transaction ID to tracking down an intermittent error. Here’s how faster lookups help engineers and AI agents follow those leads.Trace one ID across weeks of logsMost needle-in-a-haystack searches start from a single identifier: a customer ID from a support ticket, a failing transaction from a payment alert, or a trace ID copied from a slow span.With full-text search, the line filter you already use is the fast path:{service="payments"} |= "txn-123456"Loki no longer has to read every chunk in the stream selector across the whole time range. The index sends it to the data that can contain txn-123456. You can search a wider time range with a broader stream selector and still get results fast enough to stay focused.Anyone on the on-call rotation can paste an ID, set a long time range, and get an answer. You no longer need a Loki expert to make that query efficient.Hunt down rare and intermittent errorsSome of the hardest incidents to investigate never show up on a dashboard. An error shows up a few times a day on a few hosts, and the only evidence is a specific string buried in the logs.Full-text search speeds up literal and case-insensitive searches, so you can look across services for rare errors without knowing in advance where they'll appear:{service="api"} |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"You can also combine literals to narrow results while staying on the fast path:{service="api"} |= "txn-123456" |~ "(?i)webhook signature mismatch"You find the first occurrence of an intermittent failure faster, which makes it easier to tie that failure to a deploy, a dependency, or a specific customer.Speed up AI-driven investigations Fast lookups matter even more as AI agents take on more of the investigation work. AI-driven investigations often run many queries in a row: an agent checks a hypothesis, searches for an ID, follows it into another service, and searches again. Faster needle-in-a-haystack queries mean each of those steps returns sooner, so the investigation keeps moving.Get startedIf you use Grafana Cloud Logs, full-text search is available now at no additional cost. You don't need to change ingestion, redesign labels, or learn a new query language.Try full-text search in your stack, or create a free Grafana Cloud account to get started today.  To run your first search:Open Explore in your Grafana Cloud stack and choose your Grafana Cloud Logs data source.Pick a stream selector and add a line filter for a value you'd normally search for, such as a request ID, customer ID, or error string.Set a longer time range than you'd usually risk, such as the last few days or weeks, and run the query.For supported query patterns and best practices, see the full-text search documentation.Faster search is one way we’re helping teams get more value from their logs. At ObservabilityCON 2026, we also announced Adaptive Logs updates to give you more control over storage costs. To learn more, check out this on-demand talk from the event.

title: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience
description: Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7.We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below.Starting with why“Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella MeadowsAt Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible.Meanwhile, over the last year, the product design team has worked with our engineers to build new interaction patterns to support AI solutions like Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace. Building these patterns opened the door to curiosity, and we started experimenting with new visual forms, colors, shapes, and effects that laid the groundwork for the refresh.Through this work, our approach to UI style and aesthetics evolved, and so did our purpose: alongside supporting new workflows and use cases, we wanted to bring greater consistency to interactions and design patterns across Grafana. This refresh is the first step toward that goal.Visual styling and usability“The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its usefulness.” – Dieter RamsSo why invest in visual styling? To stay relevant? To facilitate sales conversations? Because it looks cool?All of those reasons are valid, but at Grafana Labs, product designers are utilitarians first. We believe digital products should exist with a clear purpose and function in mind. We think each color, font style, and line should establish a clear information hierarchy and help users quickly understand what's on the page, ultimately making our product easier to use.As more workflows shift to terminals and agentic chat interfaces, we believe investing in visual style now is foundational to Grafana’s future usability. When fewer user journeys rely on a traditional UI, those that do must emphasize clarity and consistency.What’s new: a closer look This first phase of the refresh focuses on making the Grafana UI clearer and more consistent across workflows and components, while giving you time to adapt to the changes. Here are some of the highlights:New default light and dark themes: These themes use completely new color palettes with improved accessibility compliance by design.Increased consistency across components: We have started to reduce the amount of available UI components and their variants. This means users only need to learn an interaction or a pattern once, and can then leverage it across the entire platform.New font styles, borders, and shadows: By overhauling our visual primitives to work in a proportional and scalable way, we create layers of hierarchy and visual information. As part of our audits, we noticed that many areas of the UI competed for users’ attention. We’re moving to a state where you can immediately understand what’s most important on a page, so you can complete tasks faster and more efficiently. You’ll notice these changes across the building blocks of Grafana, including cards, panels, and drawers.We’re rolling out the visual refresh gradually so Grafana contributors and users have time to adapt without disrupting critical workflows. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Existing navigation stays the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous styling at any time.For a full list of changes in the public preview, please visit our documentation.Curiosity, monitoring, and feedback"There are three key practices needed in order to build and maintain a circle of competence: curiosity and a desire to learn, monitoring, and feedback." – Shane Parrish & Rhiannon BeaubienCuriosity is a key attribute of product designers at Grafana Labs and we knew that unifying the look and feel across Grafana meant making choices that could elicit strong reactions. This is why learning, gathering feedback, and monitoring the response have been central to our process.We could have spent a year working on what we think is a perfect new visual styling, running hundreds of internal iterations, but instead we started with early internal dogfooding of the refreshed UI. This led to honest discussions and opinions from Grafanistas across the company, helping us iterate the visual refresh rapidly into a version we could not have achieved without working openly. Now, with the refresh in public preview, your feedback is central to how we’ll continue to refine our visual styling. Through our community Slack and a temporary in-app survey, you can tell us directly what’s working, what needs improvement, and what we might have missed. We monitor and discuss this feedback in the open, helping to amplify your voice and share it across the organization. Your responses will be integral to shaping future iterations of the refresh.We can’t wait to hear what you think, and to continue our evolution toward a bolder visual experience for all Grafana users.

title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
description:
When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any
  reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such
  words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't
  in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing
  tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a
  glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available
  for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances.

The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization
  concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting
  transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations
  generate enough text to do the job.

The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of
  several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The
  generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known
  terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the
  most confusion.

Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to
  produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may
  be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative
  definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM
  can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on
  precision and conciseness.

Once we have a draft glossary, then  human experts in that domain should
  review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of
  sticks.

We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It
  should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the
  tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a
  schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents
  and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes
  over time.

Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different
  places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion
  of Bounded Context. Source code can be a particularly
  interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is
  used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of
  bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries
  for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant
  to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a
  single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a
  glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to
  highlight its different usage in different contexts.

When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare
  different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe
  differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text
  can be particularly instructive.

If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms
  and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then
  use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working.

A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering. Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that
  names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the
  enterprise. Sensors in a
  harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software
  and in the user-interface.

When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts.
  For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not
  be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be
  only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded
  context to the part of the enterprise serving them.

It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used,
  in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that
  are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate
  what period of time a term should be in effect.

In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations,
  a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the
  activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit
  context
  layers in enterprise data. Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a
  simple, but useful, part of this work.

    activity and thus inspired this post. Amy Pellegrini, Annie Luxton, Arun Srinivasan, Chris Ford, Daniel

title: Deprecating the Collector Batch Processor
description:
Batching in the OpenTelemetry Collector is a process that ensures requests
are the right size for the exporter, large enough to improve compression and
amortize round-trip latency, but not so large as to exceed limits. Batching
combines a number of concerns that are critical to performance, reliability, and
cost in running Collectors.
Since OpenTelemetry began in 2019, its Collector has included a batch
processor component, responsible for combining and splitting requests before
sending them to downstream consumers, monitoring inbound and outbound timeouts,
and holding back new requests when the pipeline is full.

title: Fragments: November 10
description:
It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar.

The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends.


  One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent.

  Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on?


Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on  the recent election’s impact on data centers.


  I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.


He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI:


  you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.


There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition.

He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming.

There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments.

To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse. He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering, in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is.


  I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data?


His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.)

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming.


  Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.


While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains (“I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights.

Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone, by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Jessica Kerr (jessitron):


  My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered.

  Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents.


  An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do.


They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context, which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at:


  Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended?
  Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done?
  Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true?
  Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters?
  Security: Should the agent have this context at all?


They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor)

I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around:


  What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use.

  70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them.


That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
description: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state. Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock? For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?The TL;DR on WatchersWatchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.Put the intelligence only where it's neededKeeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: Working out what to watch and what normal looks likeComparing the same signals with normal again and againDeciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone forOnly the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. So a watcher splits the work three ways:JobWho does itWhenDecide what to watch and what normal looks likeA calibration agent, with a capable model and toolsOnce, and again when you recalibrateFetch the data and compare it with the baselinePlain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern trackingEvery runDecide whether it matters, and explain whyA small, fast model, in a single call with no toolsEvery runAnd here's what that workflow looks like:Calibration: do the hard thinking onceCalibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.The calibration agent:Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.Run plain code, then make one model callA calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.What it costsHere's what that adds up to for the 43 Watchers running on our internal stack, at our list price of $2 per million tokens:Types of WatchersCost to run per monthMedian WatcherLess than $541 of 43 WatchersLess than $10Most expensive Watcher (43 checks, every 15 minutes)A little over $20Even the most expensive one spends less than one cent per run. Cost follows the two things you control: how often a watcher runs (every five minutes to every three hours) and how much it watches. Calibration comes on top, and investigations a watcher launches are billed as investigations. Each watcher's Overview tab estimates its monthly token usage, so you see the cost before your bill does.Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026. After that, they will draw on your plan’s monthly system-initiated allowance (shared with other automated work) and bill on Assistant token usage. See Grafana Assistant pricing for more info.Note: Watchers will work exactly as they do today when billing goes live, and we expect the cost of running one to remain in line with what we’ve shared here.What our own watcher foundA cost-effective watcher is only worth it if it catches things. Over the past few months, the watcher our team runs on Grafana Assistant itself found more than 10 production bugs that affected customers, including:A crashlooping Microsoft Teams integrationBroken investigation reportsMissing webhook credentials in a newly enabled regionSlack OAuth failuresEven bugs in Watchers themselves, like alerts that never reached AlertmanagerMany of these surfaced as a new error pattern in the logs. A new pattern alone is often noise, but one that lines up with rising errors and a fresh deploy usually isn't. That's exactly the kind of call a watcher makes well.It isn't always right about the cause, and it doesn't need to be. During one rollout, it flagged real failures from an exhausted MySQL database but blamed the wrong cause, and engineers found an expensive query plan that likely contributed. The watcher notices; people, or an Assistant Investigation, dig in.Plug it into your stackA watcher can sit on top of most of your stack:Data sources: Prometheus (including Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus), CloudWatch metrics, Loki, Tempo, Pyroscope, Synthetic Monitoring, Grafana-managed alerts, and BigQuery for business signals. With the Infinity data source, it can also read any HTTP API that returns JSON or XML. One of ours watches the status pages of the LLM providers that Assistant depends on.Destinations: Slack, Microsoft Teams, signed webhooks, and Grafana Alerting, so findings flow through your notification policies and contact points, including Grafana Cloud IRM. A critical finding can also launch an Assistant Investigation or trigger an Assistant Automation.Watchers don't replace alert rules; they cover what you can't spell out in advance. To find the right mix, ask Assistant to review a service, and it recommends an alert, a watcher, or both for each failure mode.To try it, go to AI > Watchers in Grafana Cloud and create a watcher for a service your team checks by hand after every release. Describe what normal looks like, pick your data sources, and let calibration do the rest. To learn more, refer to the Watchers documentation.

possible: you write a manifest file in YAML to select the components you care
about, and ocb compiles them into the resulting binary.
